title: Custom Properties (Variables)
summary: A CSS custom property gives a reusable name to a value, such as a colour.
introduction: A CSS custom property gives a reusable name to a value, such as a colour. Think of a paint pot labelled "main colour". Use that name in several places, then change the pot once to change them all.
learningObjectives: Declare custom properties on :root and read them with var()
Provide fallbacks and override values per component, theme or media query
Use custom properties with calc() and know what they cannot do

blocks.text: A custom property is declared like any other property, except that its name starts with two hyphens: `--brand: #1d4ed8;`. The name is case-sensitive and the value can be anything: a colour, a length, a list of fonts, even part of a shorthand. Declaring it on `:root` (the `html` element) makes it available to every element on the page. Reading it is `var(--brand)`, which the browser replaces with the current value when it computes the style.

blocks.text: Change `--brand` on the first line and run again: the link, the card border and the button all follow. That is the whole point: one decision, one place.

Custom properties are inherited, so a value set on an element is visible to all of its descendants. Set a different value on a component and every rule inside it that reads the variable picks up the new value, with no changes to those rules. This is how one button style can look right on a light card and on a dark banner.

blocks.text: `var()` accepts a second argument that is used when the property is *not defined*: `var(--card-text, #172033)`. The fallback may itself contain commas or another `var()`. What a fallback does **not** cover is a variable that is defined but holds a value the property cannot use. That declaration becomes *invalid at computed-value time*: the browser does not go back to an earlier declaration of the same property, it uses the property's inherited or initial value instead.

blocks.title: A bad value does not fall back to the previous declaration
blocks.text: With `--size: red; width: var(--size);` the browser cannot know the value is wrong until it substitutes it, long after the cascade chose that declaration over `width: 300px`. The result is `width: auto`, the initial value, and no error. When a property mysteriously resets to its default, inspect the variable's value in the developer tools' *Computed* panel.

Because the rules that *use* variables never change, theming is a matter of redefining the variables under a condition: inside `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, under a class or attribute that JavaScript toggles, or, with no JavaScript at all, under `:root:has(#dark:checked)`, which the example below uses.

blocks.text: Variables combine with `calc()` and with colour functions. A spacing scale built from one base value stays consistent, and a palette built from one hue stays harmonious. A variable can also hold a plain number: `calc(var(--columns) * 1fr)` is not valid, but `calc(100% / var(--columns))` is, and `calc(var(--n) * 1px)` is the standard way to attach a unit to a unitless value.

blocks.title: Registering a variable so it can animate
Naming
blocks.text: Name variables after their *role*, not their value: `--color-accent`, `--space-m`, `--radius-card`. When the accent changes from blue to green the name still makes sense, and a reader can tell what a value is for without opening the declaration.

questions.question: Site-wide custom properties are usually declared on the `___` selector so that every element inherits them.
questions.explanation: `:root` matches the `html` element, the ancestor of everything on the page, so values declared there are inherited everywhere.
